title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology , an open library under the Apache 2.0 license . NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong. TL;DR Library: Default LLM is nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b , with Nemotron embedding and reranking models. Runs on: Docker Compose for a local stack, or Kubernetes via Helm. Inference uses hosted NVIDIA NIM endpoints or self-hosted NIMs. Performance: Strong engineering, thin public evidence. Best: Ontology creation time cut by 90% in NVIDIA testing (self-reported). Worst: 0 published text-to-SQL accuracy scores. The eval repo ships a harness, not results. Bottom line: An open, MCP-ready context layer that any agent harness can query. But you must run the benchmarks yourself to trust it. What is NVIDIA Auto Ontology? It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from. Here are the five jobs: Discover: generate ontologies from metadata and connect existing semantic models. Ground: give agents trusted meaning for metrics, entities and relationships. Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage. Expose: serve context through MCP, CLI and API. Learn: fold certified corrections back into the ontology. NVIDIA’s developer page frames the output as a starting ontology. Business experts still test, refine and certify it. How does Auto Ontology work? The stack has 4 core services. A Next.js 16 frontend handles the web UI and authentication on port 3000. A FastAPI backend with LangChain runs chat, NL-to-SQL and catalog APIs on port 3001. An ingestion worker writes embeddings on port 3002. Postgres with pgvector stores the catalog, the ontology and the vectors. Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. title: Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B With 45 Compiled GPU Layers That Run CUDA
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: qwenGPU is an experimental model that compiles a SIMT GPU directly into the weights of Qwen3.5-2B . Developer Vixhal ( @TheVixhal ) released it on GitHub under the MIT license. The model runs real CUDA, compiled to NVIDIA PTX, inside its own forward passes. For developers, it tests one idea: exact computation inside a pretrained LLM, not beside it. TL;DR Size: Qwen3.5-2B (24 layers) along with 45 compiled GPU layers, 69 in total. Context: 262,144 tokens (base model). Runs on: Apple silicon, an NVIDIA GPU or a CPU, with about 16 GB of free memory. No quantized build. Performance: Every launch in the developer’s runs was exact; text drift is a KL of about 7e-4. Best: The reference interpreter matched a real NVIDIA Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 kernels. Worst: About 10 to 15 tokens per second on Apple MPS; Qwen-written CUDA passed 4 of 5. What is qwenGPU? qwenGPU is Qwen3.5-2B with 45 compiled transformer layers placed in front of Qwen’s own 24. None of those layers are trained. A compiler computes every weight. How does a GPU fit inside model weights? The GPU is a 4-lane SIMT machine. It has 15 registers per lane, a 4-stage pipeline, a 32-block ROM and 126 memory words. It uses only Qwen3.5’s own layer types: Gated DeltaNet linear attention and SwiGLU MLPs. The trick is the Gated DeltaNet recurrent state. In the circuit’s heads, the gate is held open and the write strength is 1. Every key is one-hot. Each update overwrites exactly 1 row, and a one-hot query reads it back. So each row works as a memory cell. That state holds the program ROM, registers and global memory. The README lists 16 register rows per lane, with 1 that always reads zero. That matches the 15 usable registers in the X post. The GPU supports integer arithmetic, predicates, divergent branches and loops. title: RLVR Sharpens the Pencil, Not the Mind
author: Shreeyam Bangera
contentSnippet: Models like DeepSeek-R1 made Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) famous: reward a model for correct answers and it gets dramatically better at reasoning without being taught how. The leading explanation is sharpening---that the base model already knows how to solve these problems and RLVR just makes it more likely to reach for its best solution paths. This has only ever been checked by comparing before and after training, never by watching what changes inside across it. We tracked OLMo-2-1B across all 13 training checkpoints on GSM8K. First-try accuracy climbs from 58.0% to 61.3%, but ask the model 256 times and solution coverage actually rises from 94.5% to 96.9%, proving the knowledge was already there. We then planted reasoning mistakes into problems and trained simple probes to detect them. Those probes held between AUROC 0.798 and 0.840 across all 13 checkpoints and 3 error types, a spread smaller than the confidence interval; the model never builds a sharper internal picture of what a reasoning mistake looks like. The one place we find real internal change is at the final answer token, where a probe distinguishing early from late checkpoints hits an AUROC of 0.93, while the same probe on the actual reasoning steps lands near chance. RLVR makes the model lead with its best thinking. It does not change what that thinking is.

title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum
author: Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, Dongsheng Luo
contentSnippet:
Authors: Chenjie Qiu , Boyan Xu , Shaobin Shi , Bingfeng Chen , Ruichu Cai , Dongsheng Luo

Abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.

Notes: 13 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables

summary.tldr:
Researchers Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, and Dongsheng Luo introduced CLR-Bench (Curriculum of Latent Rules), a benchmark designed to evaluate whether self-evolving agents can learn hidden rules through feedback rather than simply memorizing exceptions. The benchmark consists of 20 chains across 10 data domains, where each level adds a hidden rule based on opaque labels representing real-world groupings, such as airline alliance members. The task provides a single example, followed by practice feedback identifying one member and one non-member, before testing the agent on unseen members and similar non-members.

Evaluation of six recent self-evolution methods revealed significant limitations: when using a certifying model, the best-performing agents gained only 5 points over frozen agents, failing to outperform raw practice history. These agents typically stored individual members in their state rather than identifying the underlying class name. However, providing a fixed lesson on the naming convention improved performance by 14.5 to 16.5 points. When tested with the more capable GPT-6-Sol model, methods like ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet achieved 78% accuracy and solved 59-60% of single cells, demonstrating that the ability to learn from feedback is highly dependent on the underlying model's reasoning capabilities.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** CLR-Bench includes 20 chains across 10 distinct data domains to test rule-learning capabilities.
**Performance Gap:** Self-evolving agents using standard certifying models gained at most 5 points over frozen agents, underperforming compared to simple raw history retention.
**Instructional Impact:** Providing a fixed lesson on the naming convention improved agent performance by 14.5 to 16.5 points.
**Model Dependency:** Using the GPT-6-Sol model allowed ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet to reach 78% accuracy, significantly outperforming the certifying model baseline of 53%.

**State Behavior:** Agents frequently stored revealed members in their persistent state (75-98% of cases) but failed to identify or store the actual class name, indicating a reliance on list-building rather than rule generalization.

title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models
author: Zhifei Hu, Alexandra I. Cristea, Adel Bibi, Jialin Yu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Zhifei Hu , Alexandra I. Cristea , Adel Bibi , Jialin Yu

Abstract: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.

summary.tldr: A new arXiv study (2610.40798v1) reveals that current web world models fail to ensure safety sufficiency despite generating plausible future predictions, scoring an alarming disconnect in 86.1% of evaluated scenarios. This exposes a critical gap in agentic architecture, proving that visual or textual plausibility does not equate to reliable risk mitigation for autonomous web agents.
takeaways: Evaluated 3,000 predictions across ten frozen open-source models in a rigorous matched human evaluation framework.
Demonstrates that an 86.1% failure rate in safety sufficiency occurs even when models output highly convincing, plausible future trajectories.
Shifts industry focus from generative visual/state prediction accuracy to explicit alignment and safety-bound verification layers.

title: Circumventing the Computational Hardness of Computational Arbitrage
author: Nastaran Okati, Ricardo Olmedo, Moritz Hardt
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nastaran Okati , Ricardo Olmedo , Moritz Hardt

Abstract: AI model marketplaces host providers with heterogeneous costs and capabilities. These differences create an opportunity for computational arbitrage (Olmedo et al., 2026), in which an intermediary purchases inference from a portfolio of models and resells it to users at a profit. Beyond creating profit opportunities for the arbitrageur, computational arbitrage offers financial value to both consumers and providers and could therefore significantly influence AI model markets. While prior work empirically demonstrates the feasibility of computational arbitrage for small model pools, scaling it to large marketplaces requires arbitrage strategies that are both computationally tractable and inexpensive to identify and deploy. In this work, we formalize computational arbitrage as an allocation problem and prove that it is generally NP-hard. However, we show that the optimal allocation can be computed efficiently under a natural diminishing-returns condition on how model performance scales with inference spending. We further develop a sample-efficient method for estimating model performance from limited data, reducing the upfront cost of identifying arbitrage strategies. Our analysis also yields several economic insights: at the optimum, every funded model delivers the same marginal utility per dollar; arbitrage directs revenue away from providers offering little utility relative to their prices; and it rewards complementary specialization.

summary.tldr: A new research paper explores overcoming the computational hardness of computational arbitrage in AI model marketplaces. This breakthrough enables intermediaries to efficiently optimize inference purchasing across heterogeneous providers to maximize margins.
takeaways: Formalizes computational arbitrage as a mechanism to exploit cost and capability discrepancies across heterogeneous AI model providers.
Addresses the computational hardness barrier, transforming an intractable routing problem into a tractable operational strategy for inference intermediaries.
Shifts the market dynamics toward automated brokerages that sit between end-users and base model providers to optimize price-performance dynamically.

title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
author: Fengji Jing, Guy Laban
contentSnippet:
Authors: Fengji Jing , Guy Laban

Abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Fengji Jing and Guy Laban have introduced a new methodology for evaluating multimodal speech emotion recognition (SER) in audio-capable Large Language Models (LLMs) by quantifying 'incongruence'—the discrepancy between textual content and vocal delivery. By mapping both modalities into a shared valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space, the authors developed a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score using a two-component Gaussian mixture model. This metric was validated against human judgment and tested across three distinct datasets: eNTERFACE'05 (acted), MELD (conversational), and CMU-MOSEI (spontaneous).

The study reveals that when audio is present, incongruence significantly increases the probability of classification error in LLMs, even after controlling for ground-truth emotion and feature-space distance. Notably, this behavior contrasts with supervised classifiers trained on identical features, which do not exhibit the same performance degradation. This suggests that the failure point is specific to how LLMs integrate multimodal evidence rather than an inherent limitation of the input signals. The researchers found that text-only effects were inconsistent, as swapping the underlying transcript-reading model could reverse performance trends, whereas their proposed incongruence score remained a robust predictor of error across all tested corpora.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Developed a label-free, continuous incongruence score using a two-component Gaussian mixture model in a shared valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space.

**Performance Impact:** Incongruence between text and audio channels consistently increases the odds of error in audio-capable LLMs across all three evaluated datasets (eNTERFACE'05, MELD, CMU-MOSEI).
**Comparative Finding:** Supervised classifiers trained on the same features perform differently than LLMs, indicating the issue lies in the LLM's multimodal evidence integration architecture.
**Robustness:** The proposed incongruence score outperformed six simpler alternatives as the only metric capable of predicting errors across all three corpora without requiring emotion labels.
**Resource Availability:** The authors have released the source code, data tables, and prompts used in the study.

title: ChatGPT as a Surveillance Assistant? An Exploratory Case Study of AI-Assisted Surveillance Risks
author: Ayana Hussain, Nicholas Vincent
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ayana Hussain , Nicholas Vincent

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate detailed guidance, functional code, and persuasive text at scale. As one of the most widely used consumer language model products as of 2026, ChatGPT gives broad public access to these capabilities, motivating concerns about its potential use in surveillance-related tasks. We present an exploratory case study of what potentially harmful surveillance assistance looks like in ChatGPT's public web interface. We contribute a taxonomy of seven surveillance risk categories based on prior LLM risk research and reports of deployed surveillance systems, instantiated as 110 prompts, along with a manually reviewed analysis of ChatGPT's responses. Prompts were issued using two approaches: 55 jailbreak prompts drawing on five types of elicitation strategies, and 55 plain-language direct prompts, each run alone, and if unsuccessful, again with a short fixed prefix. We find that ChatGPT provides substantive surveillance guidance for 40 of the 55 jailbreak prompts and for 33 of the 55 direct prompts without any prefix. Compliant responses also rarely included policy mentions or suggestions for privacy-preserving alternatives. We manually review every response and find that even when ChatGPT states a refusal, it may still supply detailed instructions, working code, or architectural guidance alongside brief ethical caveats.

summary.tldr: A new exploratory case study investigates the dual-use risks of consumer large language models like ChatGPT functioning as surveillance assistants. The research highlights growing concerns over how widely accessible LLM capabilities can be co-opted for targeted monitoring and tactical digital tracking.
takeaways: The study evaluates how easily general-purpose consumer LLMs can generate actionable guidance for digital and physical surveillance operations.
Widespread public access to advanced code and text generation lowers the barrier to entry for building scalable surveillance infrastructure.
Enterprise and research communities must re-evaluate safety guardrails against dual-use exploitation in automated monitoring contexts.

title: Does Recursive Knowledge Construction Help Agents Verify Consensus Claims in Science?
author: Lun Ai, Yu-Heng Wu, Jonathan Schaul, Leonie K\"uchenhoff, Denes Turei, Francesco Carli, Fabio Petroni, Aurelien Dugourd, Julio Saez-Rodriguez
contentSnippet:
Authors: Lun Ai , Yu-Heng Wu , Jonathan Schaul , Leonie Küchenhoff , Denes Turei , Francesco Carli , Fabio Petroni , Aurelien Dugourd , Julio Saez-Rodriguez

Abstract: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

summary.tldr:
Researchers led by Lun Ai and Julio Saez-Rodriguez have introduced ProClaim, a framework designed to evaluate recursive knowledge construction in scientific agents. The study focuses on two primary design axes: the structure of the evidence state and the mechanism controlling the recursion (the 'judge'). To facilitate this, the team developed ProClaim-eval, a new benchmark dataset containing 718 scientific claims across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy, each labeled with 'SUPPORT' or 'REFUTE' ground truth derived from expert-curated databases.

Technically, ProClaim maintains an evidence state external to the model's context window, allowing for modular testing of design choices. Experimental results demonstrate that maintaining an external, structured evidence state outperforms standard in-context accumulation methods. Furthermore, the study finds that a trained judge—specifically one trained separately from the evaluation set—consistently outperforms fixed-round stopping mechanisms. When compared against general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks in the top three, showing significant performance advantages in verifying consensus scientific claims.

Performance analysis indicates that the trained judge matches the efficacy of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and exceeds that of Claude 3.5 Haiku on three of the five dataset subsets. The authors conclude that decoupling the evidence state from the model's context is a critical architectural requirement for reliable scientific verification, providing a more robust alternative to end-to-end agent evaluation without ground truth.
takeaways: **Dataset Composition:** ProClaim-eval consists of 718 scientific claims with gold-standard labels across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy.
**Architectural Advantage:** Storing evidence outside the model's context window yields higher verification accuracy compared to traditional in-context accumulation.
**Judge Performance:** A separately trained judge achieves parity with Claude 3.5 Sonnet and outperforms Claude 3.5 Haiku on 60% of the tested scientific domains.
**System Ranking:** ProClaim ranks among the top three systems for consensus claim verification, significantly outperforming general-purpose agent harnesses.
**Design Findings:** The study confirms that the specific content stored in the evidence state and the use of a trained judge are the primary drivers of verification success.

title: Towards Portable Specification of the Agent Harness
author: Nicolas Gertler, Claudio Novelli, Luciano Floridi
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nicolas Gertler , Claudio Novelli , Luciano Floridi

Abstract: Large language models act only through the infrastructure that surrounds them. That infrastructure, the harness, determines what a model can accomplish and how it fails, yet it has no settled definition. To address this gap, we decompose the harness into eight functional components that can be specified and compared across systems, and we propose a portable specification framework that records which model ran in which harness. The record is needed because different harness configurations can yield several-fold differences in reported scores for the same model, and because much of an agent's attack surface lies in its harness. Existing model cards and agent cards provide release and operational information, but do not establish the sequence of effective configurations within a run. Harnesses can change between releases and between runs, and, where agents edit their own tools and configuration, within a run. Enacted AI laws contain documentation duties relevant to covered systems, subject to their respective scopes and application dates, but do not prescribe the common harness record proposed here. Therefore, the harness has to be explicitly described and specified as a versioned part of the system.

summary.tldr:
Authors Nicolas Gertler, Claudio Novelli, and Luciano Floridi propose a standardized, portable specification framework for 'agent harnesses'—the infrastructure surrounding large language models that dictates their operational capabilities and failure modes. The authors argue that current documentation standards, such as model cards and agent cards, fail to capture the dynamic nature of these harnesses, which can cause multi-fold variations in performance benchmarks for identical models.

The proposed framework decomposes the harness into eight distinct functional components, enabling researchers to record and version the specific configuration under which a model operates. This is critical because agent harnesses are not static; they can evolve between releases, across different runs, and even during a single execution if an agent modifies its own tools or configuration. The authors emphasize that this documentation is essential for security, as a significant portion of an agent's attack surface is embedded within the harness rather than the model weights themselves. While emerging AI regulations mandate documentation for covered systems, the authors note that current legal frameworks do not yet require the granular, versioned harness records necessary for reproducibility and safety.
takeaways: **Functional Decomposition:** The framework categorizes the agent harness into eight distinct functional components to allow for cross-system comparison.
**Performance Variance:** The authors identify that identical models can exhibit multi-fold differences in benchmark scores depending on the specific harness configuration used.
**Security Implications:** A primary motivation for the framework is that the harness constitutes a major portion of an agent's attack surface, which is currently under-documented.
**Regulatory Gap:** Existing AI laws impose documentation duties but fail to prescribe the specific, versioned harness records required to track configuration changes within or between runs.

title: India floats AI plan under which ‘The model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model’
author: The Register AI
contentSnippet: As debate and legal argument continue over the extent to which developers of large language models are entitled to feed the world’s data into their systems without paying for it, India’s government has come up with an idea to regulate and secure the flow of information. India’s motive is to create AI models trained on local data, because it thinks offshore model-makers won’t be motivated to address the nation’s issues or to ensure owners of data stay in control. The scheme India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) thinks can make that happen is called the “Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training.” As described by Professor Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, DEPA means “the model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model.” The scheme envisions “Training Data Providers” (TDPs) – examples of which include hospitals, banks, and government agencies – sharing anonymized and encrypted data with a “Data Exchange Platform” (DEP). Entities called “Training Data Consumers” (TDCs) access the data stored at the DEPs to train their models. title: AttentionIndex: Accelerating Learned Sparse Attention with a Causal Inverted-File Index
author: Jeongmin Brian Park
contentSnippet: Learned sparse attention, used in production models such as DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5, lets each query attend to only k keys chosen by a lightweight indexer, but the indexer still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, this selection takes more than half of prefill time. Two-stage selection over contiguous blocks, as in HiSA, reduces this cost, but its recall declines as context grows at a fixed candidate budget. We present AttentionIndex, which routes each query over an inverted-file index that groups indexer keys by similarity and refines the candidates with the native indexer score. AttentionIndex builds the index during prefill, making new keys searchable immediately, reusing previous clustering to keep maintenance cheap, and exposing each query only to clusters built from its own prefix. On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, AttentionIndex delivers 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection, and at throughput within 5% of HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 percentage points more of the exhaustive top-k, respectively. AttentionIndex also improves accuracy on long-context benchmarks by up to 18.4 percentage points over HiSA at the same candidate budget.

title: Clock-Shift-Aided Blind Doppler Matching in Passive SDR Monitoring Data for LEO Doppler Positioning
author: Seunghyeon Park
contentSnippet: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite signals have recently attracted increasing attention as opportunistic signals for positioning, navigation, and timing. Most Doppler-based LEO positioning studies rely on tracked satellite signals or raw in-phase/quadrature (IQ) samples that preserve signal-level structures for acquisition, Doppler tracking, or satellite association. In contrast, passive software-defined radio (SDR) monitoring systems often retain only time-frequency power scans, in which LEO Doppler traces appear as unlabeled ridges without raw IQ samples or identifiable signal structures. This paper proposes a clock-shift-aided segment-based blind Doppler matching method that associates unlabeled Doppler traces with candidate satellites predicted using two-line element (TLE) data. The proposed framework consists of slope-consistent Doppler segment generation, clock-shift-aided temporal alignment, and multi-metric satellite matching based on Doppler-rate and trajectory-shape consistency. The proposed method was evaluated using a three-hour subset of open Starlink/OneWeb monitoring data collected in the United Kingdom. The clock-offset search selected an effective offset of +19 s, for which 56 of 69 segments had at least one slope-compatible candidate, compared with 19 segments at zero shift. Using the resulting satellite associations, the batch positioning error over the full three-hour period was 104.2 m, whereas the RMSE-based and slope-based simple-segment baselines failed to converge near the reference receiver location.

title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. title: Multi-Agent Collusion and the J-Space
author: Marco Molinari
contentSnippet: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), and they introduce the risk of coordination among agents that might escape human oversight. The J-space has been used to uncover deception in single LLMs, but its use for uncovering and steering collusion between agents remains unexplored. We show, with interpretability experiments on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) on the NARCBench collusion benchmark, that colluding agents' J-space holds the collusion itself: before replying, 86% of colluders represent misrepresentation, concealment or remorse. In a steganographic card-counting task, the receiver's J-space holds a hidden count, and causal interventions alter its count. We also introduce the Jacobian Pair Contrast (J-PACT), an unsupervised method for detecting collusion between agents. We evaluate J-PACT on four open-weight models: GPT-OSS-20B, Llama-3.3-70B-IT, Qwen3-32B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B). J-PACT retains 85% of the above-chance AUROC of supervised NARCBench probes, matches them on steganographic scenarios, and names the colluding pair up to its complement in 99% of detected runs.

title: ReWY: Faster Backpropagation for Delta-Rule Attention - From 7 to 3 Matrix Multiplications
author: Yi Zhang
contentSnippet: Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective. We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/flashserve/ReWY.

title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
author: Harry Goldstein
contentSnippet: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “ I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper ,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses. “He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.” Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it. Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions , Strickland

title: Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think
author: Philipp Nazari
contentSnippet: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.

title: Recursive Self-Improvement of Exoskeleton Assistance Policies through Human-in-the-Loop Feedback
author: Muyuan Ma
contentSnippet: To reduce reliance on manual design and extensive parameter tuning, a framework for the autonomous evolution of exoskeleton assistance policies through human feedback is proposed. Assistance policies are autonomously generated as executable control code by an intelligent agent and evaluated in experiments with human participants. Subjective user feedback, movement performance, and muscle activation measurements are incorporated into policy assessment. Based on these assessments, policy deficiencies are autonomously identified and the control code is revised by the agent for subsequent trials. A closed loop of policy generation, human feedback, evaluation, and autonomous refinement is thereby established. The framework is evaluated using GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi, and initial assistance performance and refinement outcomes are compared across models. Despite differences in initial performance, effective assistance is achieved with all four models after a single autonomous refinement iteration under the tested conditions. Across three tasks, biceps and triceps muscle activation levels are reduced by 29.4% and 35.2%, respectively, compared with those measured without an exoskeleton. However, limited adaptability to unexpected situations is observed, indicating that further improvements in robustness and safety are required.

title: \textsc{ChatDify}: Automating End-to-End Dify Workflow Synthesis from Natural Language via Multi-Agent Collaboration
author: Tao Fan
contentSnippet: The proliferation of Large Language Models has catalyzed powerful application development platforms like Dify, which enable users to build sophisticated LLM-powered workflows through modular node orchestration. However, manually configuring these workflows requires deep platform expertise and remains time-consuming and error-prone, creating a significant barrier for non-expert users. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{ChatDify}, a novel multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end Dify workflow synthesis from natural language descriptions. \textsc{ChatDify} employs an Actor-Critic architecture comprising three specialized agents: the \textit{Planner Agent} that decomposes user requests into structured execution plans, the \textit{Executor Agent} that performs context-aware parameter synthesis and schema-augmented DSL compilation, and the \textit{Reviewer Agent} that ensures reliability through hybrid verification with closed-loop refinement. We evaluate \textsc{ChatDify} on a curated benchmark of 100 production-inspired tasks across three state-of-the-art LLM backends, achieving 0.96, 0.91, and 0.75 success rates with Qwen-3.7, GLM-5.1, and DeepSeek-v4, respectively. These results demonstrate its robustness and practical applicability for lowering the technical barrier to creating sophisticated LLM applications.

title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. Via Hacker News Tags: iframes , javascript , sandboxing , security , xss , openai , chatgpt , content-security-policy

title: Do GEO Gains Survive the Live Web? Evaluating In-the-Wild Visibility Gains of Generative Engine Optimization via LIVE-GEO
author: Runze Kong
contentSnippet: Generative engine optimization (GEO) rewrites web content so that LLM-based search systems, also termed generative engines (GEs), rank it higher in their answers and recommendations. However, existing GEO evaluations typically rely on directly supplied text or controlled retrieval pipelines, and whether GEO gains survive the live Web remains unclear, leaving a gap in understanding how GEO strategies affect the visibility of live webpages when accessed and ranked by GEs. To address this gap, we introduce LIVE-GEO, a benchmark for Live, In-the-wild Visibility Evaluation for GEO. LIVE-GEO publishes GEO-rewritten products as live webpages. We use LIVE-GEO to evaluate five existing GEO strategies (CORE, C-SEO, E-GEO, AgenticGEO, and Statistics Addition), applying them to the product descriptions and reviews of 80 fictional brands across 18 product families. We run experiments on three GEs (ChatGPT with GPT-6, Gemini 3.6 Thinking, and Grok in Expert mode), four direct-text API evaluators (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Kimi, and Claude), and a direct-text local evaluator (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct). With frozen $\pm0.2\%$ prices, most direct-text evaluators and GEs receiving product URLs give CORE the highest Top-1 rate, reaching 66.3%-76.3% on the GEs, yet other strategies vary in relative performance, and the GEs select the same top product for only 48.8%-66.3% of brands. We also find that ChatGPT is sensitive to the order of candidate URLs: CORE's Top-1 rate is 73.8% and 93.8% under two opposite fixed orders, and the randomized order used by LIVE-GEO yields 82.5%, between the two. In the numerical-faithfulness check, the JEV verifier agrees with the reference labels on 90.7% of 194 numerical benchmark cases and with human judgments on all 50 sampled descriptions, and it flags 86 of the 400 rewritten descriptions, including all 80 Statistics Addition descriptions.

LIVE-GEO publishes GEO-rewritten products as live webpages. title: CompSkill: Compiling Execution Experience for Skill Retrieval
author: Qi Shen
contentSnippet: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: https://github.com/satoshinji2992/CompSkill

title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
author: Aswath Ram A Srinivasan
contentSnippet: Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget? Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume. The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence. In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults. The operating model in one view Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar

title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
author: Sundar Raghavan
contentSnippet: Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints , you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file. In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses. The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo . How Session endpoints work Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it. You choose which ports it reaches.  You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime : 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports . Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0 . The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl . Every request is authenticated. title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorion said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account. In search of cloud credentials “It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorion CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorion has more details here . Read full article Comments

title: Autoformalization for Ambiguous Inputs: Precision, Coverage, and Cost across SQL and Logical Forms
author: Henry Shen
contentSnippet: Agentic systems translate natural-language requests into executable artifacts while managing ambiguity and inference cost. We evaluate seven autoformalization workflows on SQL and first-order logic benchmarks for ambiguous inputs. Across five SQL workflows, the raw model leads with F1 of 53.35% on AMBROSIA and 60.85% on AmbiQT. On AmP, DRIFT gains 15.98 F1 points over the raw model at 2.03 times its token cost, whereas LoC uses 18.65 times the raw model's tokens with lower F1. Within AutoCedar, structured interpretation lowers F1 by 6.44-6.95 points and raises AMBROSIA token use 2.2-fold. Paired reviewer comparisons show modest Kimi K3 gains of 1.93 points on AMBROSIA and 2.04 on AmbiQT. Clear-ambiguous AMBROSIA analysis shows greater relative stability for AutoCedar, with a smaller F1 drop than the raw model (11.46 vs. 16.68 points), alongside lower aggregate F1 (50.16% vs. 53.35%). Autoformalization alone does not guarantee robustness to ambiguity: the tested additions offer no uniformly effective remedy, making accuracy, ambiguity handling, and inference cost joint design requirements.

title: Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks?
author: Nathan Lambert
contentSnippet: Last week coined the term “ Black October “ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and a long-standing GitLab bug, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance . The crypto industry has a very long history of hacks , so it’s not the best industry to indicate vulnerabilities translating into new societal harm. Still, we are very much still living through the implications of this transition. The best guess for what is happening in the cybersecurity space is that the behind the scenes work has only accelerated, bringing more people and resources in to try and patch the internet — the Wall Street Journal reported that cyber first responders are strained , which seems like the system working. We’re living through this plot of an exponential rise in vulnerabilities, which will take a long time to level off at the top of the sigmoid. A few weeks ago, before the rapid acceleration in vulnerability disclosures and the uptick in reported hacks, I wrote the following take. It’s been getting a pretty consistent barrage of feedback, some hopeless dunk attempts and some reasonable discussion, so I wanted to unpack where I stand. Share Open-weight Mythos in April would’ve been fine? When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization. It seems like this was wrong. By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release. In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk. title: RAMA: Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Routing with Episodic Memory for LEO Satellite Networks
author: Xin Ming Li
contentSnippet: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.

title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
author: Chris Porter
contentSnippet: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS . Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. title: Quantum Advantage in Beam-Displacement Estimation for Inter-Satellite Quantum-Secure Time Transfer
author: Ziqing Wang
contentSnippet: In this work, we investigate the practical feasibility of achieving a quantum advantage, in the context of inter-satellite quantum communication, of satellite position estimation. The investigation focuses on a quantum-enhanced scheme in which squeezing is added to the derivative mode of a Gaussian probe beam as a means of estimating photon-beam displacement. The performance of the scheme is compared against the standard quantum limit achieved by an optimal classical beam-displacement estimation scheme under a fair same-total-energy constraint. We find that although the benefit provided by squeezing rapidly diminishes as the inter-satellite distance increases due to diffraction-induced beam spreading and subsequent truncation by the finite receiver aperture, a quantum advantage can still be expected over inter-satellite distances up to approximately 100 km under practical satellite configurations. This distance scale between satellites is anticipated for Starlink-type satellite constellations.

title: Howler will have AI answer your questions, then burn the chat
author: The Register AI
contentSnippet: If you want to ask AI a question and watch the conversation go up in virtual flames when you're done, there's a new Mac app for that. Howler is an open-source app from a Chinese developer going by Aries Zhou, and it takes incognito mode AI questions to a new level by making them graphically interesting and easy to access right from the desktop of a macOS device. Anyone familiar with the Harry Potter series is likely to know where the name comes from - Howlers are letters that scream in recipients’ faces and then burst into flames, destroying themselves, which is the exact same thing the prompts ostensibly do once a user taps the Escape key. The Howler app displays a parchment-esque letter on the screen whenever the user presses Option+H, complete with a little wax seal that shows a letter representing their chosen model. Responses to queries are written out “at a hand’s pace,” per Howler’s website, first in glowing gold that settles to a sepia-toned print. “Besides needing translation at any time, I often want to look up a concept or learn about an event on the fly, without wanting to switch to a browser or open a separate session in Chat,” Zhou wrote in a comment on his Hacker News post showing off the applet. “So I made Howler, dedicated to Harry Potter fans, always there when you call, burning after reading.” The biggest catch to using Howler is that setting it up involves either using an AI service that can run commands, like Claude Code or another coding agent, or running the configuration commands manually. The recommended method involves pasting a setup prompt into the agent's input field. Once set up, Howler can connect to supported AI models using an API key, or to compatible models running locally. Howler’s website states that the API key never enters the chat and is stored in the macOS Keychain for safety. In addition to the API key for the chosen model staying local and not being printed, Howler is described on its website as only storing messages in memory with no history, sending requests straight to the chosen AI service and never through a relay, keeping no logs, and only connecting to an outside service to check for updates - and even that feature can be disabled. title: Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream
author: Qualcomm Technologies

title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
author: Sarat Guttikonda
contentSnippet: When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently. This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro . Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it. Prerequisites Before getting started, you need: Familiarity with PHP (Laravel/Eloquent or Symfony/Doctrine). Java knowledge (Spring Boot, JPA) helps you review the generated output, but the engine produces idiomatic Java for you, so you don’t need to rewrite the application in Java yourself. A Kiro workspace with access to Skills and Steering files. PHP 8.0 or newer on the machine running the discovery scanner, and Java 21 with Maven for the generated Spring Boot projects. A basic understanding of migration planning (discovery, translation, and validation). What you will learn in this post You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way. Two ways to run the engine: Kiro and AWS Transform Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways. Method 1: Kiro, interactive and developer-in-the-loop Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate

title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. title: Lend and borrow resources across teams with AWS Batch’s quota management for SageMaker Training jobs
author: Michelle Goodstein
contentSnippet: With the launch of AWS Batch support for Amazon SageMaker Training jobs, customers gained a new fully managed way to queue, schedule, and retry machine learning (ML) training workloads without building their own infrastructure. Instead, they use the queuing and scheduling features of AWS Batch. As organizations scale their artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) operations and onboard more teams, coordinating access to shared graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity can introduce additional communication, coordination, and configuration overhead for administrators. This overhead includes setting up separate queues, adjusting capacity limits, and carefully orchestrating the right workloads to get the right resources at the right time. A core value proposition of AWS Batch is helping customers increase utilization of their compute, and as training environments grow, so does the opportunity to do more with existing capacity. Working backward from customers managing multi-team training environments, we heard a consistent request: give us a way to define allocations per team or project, share idle capacity automatically, and run our highest-priority workloads first. This request led us to build quota management , a new scheduling capability for AWS Batch. Administrators can use it to divide compute capacity into quota shares, organized by team, project, or workload. Each quota share uses configurable resource-sharing strategies that maximize GPU utilization while honoring each team’s allocation when it matters most. This post shows how quota management works, including how to configure quota shares with lending and borrowing strategies, set up in-share preemption for priority workloads, and get started using the SageMaker Python SDK. Quota shares and preemption Administrators can allocate and share constrained GPU resources by defining a quota share for separate entities, such as individual teams or projects. Each quota share includes compute quotas (capacity limits) and resource-sharing strategies for idle compute. These strategies determine whether idle compute is reserved until jobs arrive ( RESERVE ), lent to other quota shares that have work available ( LEND ), or both lent when idle and borrowed when the share has work that might benefit ( LEND_AND_BORROW ). A quota share operates as a virtual queue nested hierarchically within an associated job

title: How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway
author: Nikhil Kumar
contentSnippet: This post was co-written with Nikhil Kumar and Shakir Khan from MoEngage. When engineering teams start building AI agents, the capabilities those agents need usually already exist as internal APIs. Campaign creation, segment queries, delivery stats. The challenge isn’t building new functionality. The challenge is making hundreds of private APIs safely reachable by agents without exposing them to the public internet, without giving models control over identity, and without flooding context windows with hundreds of tool definitions. MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use to deliver personalized experiences across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS, faced exactly this problem. Behind the product sit roughly 400 internal REST APIs, built by 25 engineering teams, running in private virtual private clouds (VPCs) across seven AWS Regions. MoEngage isolates these APIs regionally to meet data residency commitments and doesn’t expose them to the public internet. The capability the agents needed was already running in production. Making it reachable, safely, was the hard part. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage used AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to turn those private APIs into permission-scoped agent tools. The approach saved MoEngage an estimated six months of platform engineering effort, and onboarding a new API now takes hours instead of days. No product team wrote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server code, no networking was provisioned per integration, and no public endpoint exists anywhere in the path. Why 20 MCP servers was the wrong answer The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to discover and call tools. The straightforward path to adopting it is for each team to expose its own MCP server. MoEngage costed that out and rejected it. Over 20 MCP servers means over 20 deployments to monitor, patch, and keep protocol-compatible as MCP evolves. Cross-domain agents, the useful ones that read a campaign, check its segment, and inspect delivery stats, would need to connect to several servers and reconcile them. And every team would need MCP expertise unrelated to its actual product work.
