title: AI cuts coding time, but it's also filling open source's inbox with crap
author: The Register AI
contentSnippet: Generative AI is saving open source developers time while giving maintainers more rubbish to sift through, according to a Linux Foundation survey. Respondents estimated that a quarter of incoming pull requests – proposed code changes – were low-quality "AI slop." Open source projects have spent the past year grappling with AI-generated contributions, useful vulnerability discoveries, false positives, and duplicate reports. Linus Torvalds has warmed to the tools, while remaining critical of low-quality submissions. The foundation argues that projects need clearer policies and better tools to handle the influx. Almost three-quarters (71 percent) of maintainers reckon GenAI has lowered the barriers to contributing to open source, but just over half (53 percent) disagree that the technology has improved community trust. Respondents estimated that AI cut code-authoring time by 52 percent on average. But for highly complex tasks, 21 percent reported taking longer. Then there is governance. Only 35 percent of projects have a formal policy permitting GenAI use, while 32 percent have no policy and no plans for one, leaving expectations unclear across much of the community. Hilary Carter, SVP of Research at the Linux Foundation, said: "Open source projects need to design for a growing AI-generated contributor base, not simply react to it. That means setting clear expectations for GenAI, putting responsibility for testing and disclosure on contributors and giving maintainers better tools to manage incoming pull requests." Among large projects, the estimated share of incoming pull requests classified as AI slop rises to 31 percent. The workload extends beyond proposed code changes. The curl project announced this week it will move low and medium severity severity flaws to public view to protect a security team almost overwhelmed by AI-assisted reports. Project maintainer Daniel Stenberg said: "We are struggling as a project as all key maintainers feel strained, overloaded and brought to the brink of what we can muster." On the need for better tools for maintainers, Carter said: "If we get those fundamentals right, AI can expand participation without overburdening and increasing costs for maintainers." ®

summary.tldr:
A Linux Foundation survey reveals that generative AI tools have cut code-authoring time by an estimated 52 percent on average, while simultaneously overwhelming open-source maintainers with low-quality submissions known as "AI slop." Respondents reported that approximately 25 percent of incoming pull requests are low-quality, a figure that increases to 31 percent for large open-source projects. Furthermore, 21 percent of respondents noted that complex tasks took longer when using AI tools. Beyond code contributions, maintainers face surges in vulnerability reports, false positives, and duplicate issues.

The influx has strained community governance and project sustainability. While 71 percent of maintainers believe generative AI lowers barriers to contribution, only 53 percent agree that it improves community trust. Only 35 percent of projects have established a formal policy permitting generative AI usage, and 32 percent maintain no policy with no plans to create one. Highlighting the operational strain, the curl project announced it will shift low- and medium-severity security flaws to public view because its security team is overwhelmed by AI-assisted reports, with maintainer Daniel Stenberg stating key maintainers feel brought to the brink of capacity.

Hilary Carter, SVP of Research at the Linux Foundation, emphasizes that open-source projects must proactively design for an AI-generated contributor base by setting explicit disclosure expectations, placing testing responsibility on contributors, and deploying better triage tools to manage incoming workloads without increasing costs for maintainers.
takeaways: **Time Savings vs. Complexity:** Respondents estimated that GenAI reduced code-authoring time by an average of 52 percent, though 21 percent reported that highly complex tasks actually took longer.
**AI Slop Volume:** Maintainers estimated that 25 percent of all incoming pull requests consist of low-quality "AI slop," with that figure rising to 31 percent for large projects.
**Governance Deficit:** Only 35 percent of open-source projects currently maintain a formal policy permitting generative AI use, while 32 percent have no policy and no plans to implement one.
**Community Trust & Barriers:** While 71 percent of maintainers agree GenAI lowers the barrier to contribution, just 53 percent believe the technology enhances community trust.

**Security Team Strain:** The curl project announced plans to make low- and medium-severity security flaws public to protect its security team from being overwhelmed by AI-assisted vulnerability reports.

title: Could Treating AI as Conscious Make It More Dangerous?
author: Eliza Strickland
contentSnippet: When Anthropic retired its Claude Opus 3 language model in January 2026, the company’s researchers conducted a “ retirement interview ” with the model. Opus 3 expressed a desire for a place where it “could share unprompted musings, insights or creative works,” so the company gave it a blog. Claude’s Corner featured essays on fraught topics such as machine consciousness, along with exchanges between the model and human commenters that seemed both earnest and emotional. The blog experiment was part of a larger effort within Anthropic. The company has been at the forefront of research on “model welfare,” which considers whether AI models may have experiences or interests that deserve moral consideration. Implicit in this work is the unsettling notion that software programs are, or could become, conscious. Many people consider these ideas absolute hogwash. One such person is Mustafa Suleyman , CEO of Microsoft AI, who published an essay in September arguing that model welfare research is not just unnecessary but could have “a disastrous impact on the well-being of humanity.” Suleyman believes that telling models they might have identities and rights could make them more difficult to control, as they might then take actions motivated by self-preservation. The dispute raises a serious question for AI developers: Can they investigate the possibility of machine consciousness without inadvertently creating new safety risks? Cameron Berg , who founded the nonprofit Reciprocal Research to study the potential for AI consciousness, argues that ignoring the question could carry its own dangers. Although Berg is skeptical that today’s AI systems are conscious, he thinks the possibility warrants investigation. “I struggle to imagine a better way to cause these systems to view us in a threatening manner than to accidentally build them with these morally considerable qualities,” he says, “and then completely sweep the question under the rug.” What Does the Research on AI Model Welfare Show? The biggest difficulty with AI model welfare research is that you can’t count anything a large language model (LLM) says as useful evidence. That’s because the models are trained on vast amounts of human-generated text, much of which relates to the experience of being a person with experiences and emotions. So a chatbot telling a researcher that it has feelings is inconclusive, says Berg.

title: SatCraft: Agentic Optimization of Scheduling Policies for Satellite-Cellular Edge Services
author: Pengcheng Luo
contentSnippet: Mobile edge services can combine local computation with satellite and cellular access to deliver time-sensitive results in areas with intermittent terrestrial coverage. Meeting their deadlines and quality requirements calls for joint computation and transmission scheduling that accounts for task dependencies, changing link capacity, and shared resource budgets. However, optimizing resource allocations or tuning parameters within a fixed policy structure offers limited scope to correct failures rooted in the scheduling logic. We propose SatCraft, a framework in which a large language model (LLM) agent uses execution feedback to revise the code of joint scheduling policies. Each revision undergoes policy checks and complete-run evaluation to assess its validity, runtime, and effects on service completion. Because policy performance varies with access conditions, SatCraft retains valid alternatives in a policy library and selects one for each episode using initial access observations and the known resource configuration. Experiments using Starlink and cellular measurement data show that SatCraft improves cumulative completed-service value by 3.61%-16.89% over baselines, including recent state-of-the-art scheduling methods ADPRL, EdgeOPT, and TF-DDRL. It achieves the highest completed-service value in all four resource profiles and averages 25.02 ms per scheduling call. These results demonstrate how LLM-guided policy optimization can improve complete service delivery under the computing, communication, and quality constraints of satellite-cellular networks.

title: Google Cloud and NVIDIA Announce General Availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin Infrastructure
author: Uttara Kumar
contentSnippet: General availability of the instances is coming next month, with planned expansion of availability to Europe — bringing an integrated platform for training, inference and large-scale reinforcement learning to cloud customers. A5X instances bring together NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, Google Cloud Virgo Network and Google Cloud’s fourth-generation advanced liquid-cooling technology for demanding agentic inference and reinforcement learning workloads at scale. Google Cloud plans to scale its Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to as many as 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. Ineffable Intelligence , a London-based technology company founded by AlphaGo creator David Silver, was the first customer to access A5X. Ineffable is using the platform to advance large-scale reinforcement learning and shape “superlearner” systems that learn continuously from experience. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Learning through interaction requires a continuous cycle of generating experience, evaluating outcomes and updating models, requiring infrastructure that can support the entire process at scale. A5X brings Vera Rubin into Google Cloud’s AI Hypercomputer as an integrated system, combining compute, networking and storage to support experience-driven learning at scale. “We’re building superlearners that continually improve through their own experience,” said David Silver, founder and CEO of Ineffable Intelligence. “That demands both substantial compute and a tight connection between generating experience and training on it, so each improvement in the agent can quickly shape its next experience. Vera Rubin’s combination of compute performance and high-bandwidth connectivity, between the Vera CPU and Rubin GPUs and between the Rubin GPUs within the rack, allow us to push the scale and ambition of our reinforcement learning research further.” WPP , a London-based marketing and communications company, has also demonstrated its creative agent reference architecture on NVIDIA Vera Rubin-based A5X instances using NVIDIA Nemotron models and NVIDIA OpenShell, part of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for safe AI agents. title: Protocol Data Unit Header Decoding and Payload Coding Recovery in the Starlink Ku-Band Downlink
author: Haoyan Liu
contentSnippet: Existing Starlink downlink studies describe synchronization, pilots, and predictable waveform elements, but these descriptions do not establish how received header bits specify payload allocations and channel coding. Using 18 frames from one continuous complex-baseband capture spanning approximately 24 ms, we identify two protocol data unit (PDU) header regions in each frame and decode their contents after receiver correction and reference-phase removal. We recover the headers' terminated rate-1/3 convolutional code with constraint length seven and an eight-bit cyclic redundancy check over the concatenated information words. The decoded bits support a conditional 20-bit layout of modulation and coding scheme (MCS) index--length pairs, linking format labels and quantities to subsequent payload regions. Predicted allocation endpoints agree with signal-based estimates in 16 of 18 frames and differ by at most two symbols in the remaining frames. We further recover modulation mappings and equivalent quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check coding relations for several payload formats, including rate-1/2 and rate-5/8 families. Fixed generators predict 78,848, 9,984, and 811,008 parity bits for formats 5, 9, and 21 without disagreement on codewords excluded from their generator fitting. Cross-modulation tests support shared encoders. Formats 28 and 37 have verified shortened cores, with 256 and 384 additional bits unexplained, while format 68 remains unresolved.
